title: Capacity Bridging Conductor PRD - safety corridors & tenant isolation
body:
Purpose:
This PRD introduces the Capacity Bridging Conductor (CBC): an orchestration layer for Dedicated pools that creates short-term, observable, and policy-driven "bridges" between reserved capacity and opportunistic/backfill capacity while preserving tenant isolation and latency SLOs. The CBC is intended as a conservative, operator-friendly alternative to purely elastic burst models: it coordinates pre-authorized transient capacity, enforces safety corridors, and offers deterministic fallback behavior for tenants and platform operators.

Why this now:
- Customers expect predictable latency and cost for Dedicated commitments but also ask for controlled burst during traffic spikes (e.g., marketing launches, batch jobs).
- Existing approaches (prewarm, ad-hoc borrowing, naive oversubscribe) either risk noisy neighbors or require expensive manual ops.
- CBC aims to reduce manual escalations, shorten time-to-burst, and make degradations explicit and reversible.

Goals (success criteria):
- Reduce manual ops requests for emergency capacity by >= 60% in pilot tenants.
- Keep 99th percentile latency impact within +15% of baseline during a bridge event for high-priority lanes.
- Provide transparent chargebacks and accounting for borrowed capacity (per-minute granularity).
- Offer a predictable fallback ladder so consumer apps can implement graceful degradation.

Non-goals:
- Replacing core autoscaler that provisions long-lived capacity commitments.
- Market-facing pricing redesign (billing integration will be light initially).

Key concepts and terminology:
- Bridge: a short-lived (minutes-to-hours) allocation that links a tenant's dedicated pool to an opportunistic or shared reserve.
- Safety corridor: preconfigured constraints on a bridge (max concurrency, latency tail guard, token budget, allowed model families).
- Bridge ticket: policy + authorization object created by tenant or SRE to allow a bridge.
- Fidelity lane: quality tiers (high, medium, low) that define model variant/quantization downgrade routes as part of graceful degradation.

User stories:
1) Platform SRE: "I want to quickly route traffic for Tenant A into a bridge using a pre-approved ticket, and validate via roll-forward canary that 95th p95 latency stays within corridor."
2) Tenant dev: "I want an API to request a bridge for 45 minutes that only allows embedding workloads to borrow capacity and has an explicit charge estimate."
3) Product ops: "I want dashboards that show active bridges, headroom consumption, and which tenants are degrading to lower fidelity lanes."

System design (high level):
- Bridge controller component (new service) that:
  - Accepts bridge tickets, evaluates policy, and issues allocation requests to the capacity broker.
  - Orchestrates pre-warm and slot reservation in the opportunistic pool and communicates KV cache warming hints to runtime nodes.
  - Streams telemetry (latency, token burn, queue depth) to Console for observability and to the autoscaler for feedback.
- Safety corridor enforcement:
  - Admission controller rejects bridge if corridor constraints would be violated (e.g., insufficient headroom, conflicting tenant isolation policy).
  - Runtime enforces per-tenant runtime fences (max concurrency, per-model token cap) while bridge is active.
- Fallback ladder:
  - On breach of corridor thresholds, system executes pre-configured fallback: 1) shed non-critical requests, 2) downgrade fidelity lane, 3) redirect to warm shared model variant, 4) throttle with informative error code.

Policy surface (what tenants configure):
- MaxBridgeDuration (minutes/hours)
- AllowedModelFamilies (list of model ids)
- MaxBorrowQPS and MaxTokenBurn per-minute
- FidelityLadder (ordered list of degrade targets)
- Billing preference: charge-to-tenant | absorb (trial)

APIs (sketch):
POST /v1/dedicated/{tenant}/bridges 
  payload: {duration_minutes, max_qps, allowed_models, fidelity_ladder_id, ticket_id}
GET /v1/dedicated/{tenant}/bridges/{id}
PATCH /v1/dedicated/{tenant}/bridges/{id}  (extend/terminate)
Events: bridge.created, bridge.started, bridge.threshold_breach, bridge.terminated

Observability & UX:
- Console panel: Active bridges table, per-bridge telemetry (p50/p95/p99 latencies, token burn, headroom left, fallback events).
- SLO guardrails: visual annotation on Model/Endpoint pages when bridges are active.
- Alerts: configurable alerts for corridor breach and sudden headroom drop.
- Billing preview modal when requesting a bridge that estimates cost for requested duration and QPS.

Operational runbook (high-level):
- Normal flow: Tenant requests bridge -> CBC validates -> capacity broker provisions temporary slots -> CBC coordinates warmup -> bridge goes live -> telemetry monitored.
- On corridor breach: CBC issues the following sequence (automated):
  1) Emit bridge.threshold_breach event and notify tenant via webhook/console.
  2) Execute fidelity downgrade if configured.
  3) If breach persists, throttle non-priority requests and mark bridge for termination in 5 minutes.
  4) If termination executed, re-route failed requests per tenant's fallback policy.
- Escalation: If repeated bridges cause noisy neighbor issues, auto-flag tenant for quota review and open a ticket JIRA-DED-NOISE-{tenant}.

Metrics to track:
- number_of_bridges_started, avg_bridge_duration, peak_headroom_burn, corridor_breach_rate, degraded_request_percent, ops_escalations_count
- Business: reduction_in_manual_capacity_requests, customer_satisfaction_notes_post-burst

Pilot plan and evaluation:
- Phase 0: internal SRE-only pilot with two non-production tenants for 6 weeks (validate warmup times, telemetry completeness).
- Phase 1: invite 3 enterprise beta customers with real workloads, run for 8 weeks; compare latency tail and ops ticket volume to baseline.
- Acceptance: <=15% p99 latency regression for high lane at 95% of bridge events, and bridge ticket success rate >= 90%.

Rollout and migration considerations:
- Backwards compatibility: if tenants do nothing, CBC is opt-in.
- Migration path for customers using ad-hoc reserved borrowing: provide an SRE-run migration to convert existing manual runbooks into bridge tickets.

Security & isolation notes:
- All bridges must be authorized by tenant admin or an SRE approval flow.
- Bridge tickets are signed and TTL-limited.
- Runtime level per-tenant fences are enforced by the serving runtime (max concurrency, token quotas).
- Audit logs must record all bridge lifecycle events and the model variants used during degradation.

Dependencies and open engineering work:
- Capacity broker APIs must support transient slot reservations and per-tenant tagging (infra).
- Serving runtime needs runtime fence enforcement primitives (serving-runtime).
- Console changes (product/console) for UI and billing preview.
- Billing integration for minute-granularity accounting (finance).

Open questions / unresolved tradeoffs:
- Pricing model: pass-through vs. amortized charges for burst usage? (finance + GTM)
- Should fidelity ladders be tenant-managed or curated by Redwood? (product + research)
- How aggressive should automated termination be vs. manual SRE involvement?
- How long should pre-warm windows be for different model families? (depend on model size and observed cold-start times)

Implementation milestones (rough):
- M1 (6w): Bridge controller prototype + unit tests, minimal policy checks, internal SRE-only CLI to request bridges.
- M2 (8w): Runtime fences, capacity broker transient slot API, telemetry hooks.
- M3 (6w): Console UI + billing preview + pilot with 2 customers.
- M4 (ongoing): Iteration on fallback policies, autoscaler feedback loops, GA docs and runbooks.

Notes to self / next steps:
- Sync with infra on slot-tag semantics: need exact API signature before M1 end. (Ethan)
- Schedule model-warmup experiment with serving-runtime team to measure effective warm times per model family. (Marta)
- Draft initial billing preview formula for short-term borrow (per-token + per-minute slot surcharge). (Finance touchpoint)
- Create Confluence page for pilot onboarding checklist and preflight tests.

Appendix: short failure scenarios and desired system response:
- Scenario A: Bridge causes p99 spike on host pool -> response: throttling -> fidelity downgrade -> bridge termination if persists.
- Scenario B: Capacity broker fails to provision -> response: bubble-up error to tenant and abort bridge request; offer estimated retry ETA.
- Scenario C: Tenant abuses repeated bridges to avoid purchases -> response: automated throttle policy and ops escalation.

This draft aims to capture a pragmatic, operator-friendly mechanism for controlled burst with explicit isolation guarantees. Feedback welcome on API shape, corridor primitives, and business model assumptions.
